summary: For learners aged 12–13 (UK KS3 Biology: 'the importance of bacteria in the human digestive system'), the central goal is to overturn the 'all bacteria are germs' idea and understand the gut microbiome as a mostly beneficial, mutualistic community. Learners should name at least one thing gut bacteria do that human enzymes cannot (notably fermenting dietary fibre), explain why that matters, and give a consequence of disrupting the microbiome (e.g. by antibiotics or a fibre-poor diet). Guidance centres on an interactive 'tend the gut community' model that is proposed to make the partnership causal, supported by a reveal-based gut scene, an in-role scientist conversation for 'why' questions, and sorting/short-answer checks. Relative efficacy of these media is untested.
misconceptions: Believing all bacteria are harmful germs, rather than mostly beneficial partners.
Thinking humans digest fibre themselves, rather than relying on gut bacteria to ferment it.
Assuming antibiotics only kill 'bad' bacteria and leave the helpful community untouched.
Thinking the microbiome is fixed rather than changing with diet.
Confusing gut bacteria with the pathogens that cause food poisoning.

activities.title: Tend your gut community: two digestion tracks
steps: Feed a model gut by choosing foods: food first passes through the small intestine, where the body's own enzymes work, then reaches a model colon (large intestine) full of bacteria. Watch the two digestion tracks side by side.
Observe that the body's own enzymes break down starch, sugars and protein, but cannot digest dietary fibre. The fibre passes undigested through the small intestine into the large intestine.
Watch the bacterial community act on that same fibre, fermenting it, producing beneficial products, and raising a 'gut health' indicator.
Introduce a disruption — a course of antibiotics or a switch to a fibre-poor diet — and observe the community decline and gut health drop.

Restore fibre-rich foods and observe the model's gut health recover as bacterial diversity returns. In real people, recovery after antibiotics can be slow or incomplete, and it varies from person to person.
State in your own words why the two digestive systems complete each other.
activities.insight: Fibre, which the body's own enzymes cannot digest, is a major food source for the bacterial partners, so human enzymes and gut bacteria complement each other. The microbiome is mostly beneficial, and disrupting it can have real consequences for digestion.

activities.title: Lift-the-flap gut scene: name the roles, bust the myth
steps: Tap the large-intestine community to reveal 'trillions of mostly helpful bacteria'.
Tap the fibre to reveal that bacteria ferment fibre that human enzymes cannot digest.
Open the flap 'Are gut bacteria harmful?' to reveal 'Most are helpful partners — we depend on them.'
Add a note of one further job (e.g. helping maintain a healthy gut environment or making some vitamins).
activities.insight: Learners can name what beneficial gut bacteria do and directly confront the 'all bacteria are harmful' idea.

activities.title: Ask the microbiome scientist (enrichment)
steps: Pose your own 'why' questions to an in-role gut-microbiome scientist, e.g. 'Why does my diet change my gut bacteria?' or 'What do probiotics do?'
Follow up on answers about what the bacteria do, why fibre matters, and what disrupts them.
Summarise one thing you learned that changed or confirmed your earlier idea.
activities.insight: The microbiome is an active, curiosity-rich research area; learners can pursue open questions and have their own ideas named and probed through dialogue.

activities.title: Check it: roles, what bacteria digest, disruption consequences
steps: Answer: 'What do gut bacteria digest that we cannot?' (Answer: dietary fibre.)
Match each disruption (e.g. broad-spectrum antibiotics, fibre-poor diet) to a likely consequence (e.g. impaired digestion, diarrhoea, loss of diversity).

Respond to the diagnostic prompt: 'Adverts sell soap that kills 99.9% of all bacteria. Your large intestine is home to trillions of bacteria. Are those bacteria making you ill — and what would happen to your digestion if a strong course of antibiotics killed many of them?'
activities.insight: Learners demonstrate they can distinguish beneficial from harmful bacteria, identify fibre as what bacteria digest that we cannot, and predict consequences of disruption.

checkQuestion: Adverts sell soap that 'kills 99.9% of all bacteria' as if every microbe is the enemy. But your large intestine is home to trillions of bacteria. Are those bacteria making you ill — and what would happen to your digestion if a strong course of antibiotics wiped them out?
checkAnswer: The gut bacteria are largely beneficial (a mutualistic microbiome): they break down dietary fibre that our own enzymes cannot digest and help keep harmful microbes out. Wiping them out — for example with broad-spectrum antibiotics — can disrupt digestion, cause diarrhoea, and let harmful species take over until the microbiome recovers.
